gold.historyOfPresentIllness: The patient is a 43-year-old male presenting with right calf/lower leg cramping, tightness, swelling, and mild pain that began on <date>, while playing pickleball. He reports that while running for a ball, his foot locked, causing a sensation of muscle tension extending up the leg. Symptoms have not been improving, and the right calf remains very tight with mild pain. He denies heel or knee pain.

instructions: Patient Education: Understanding Right Lower Leg Pain, Understanding Your Lower Leg Muscle Strain, Localized swelling, mass and lump, right lower limb

Your diagnosis: A strain (pull/tear) of the muscles in the back of your right lower leg (calf). This happened while you were playing pickleball. Your leg X-ray showed no broken bone. This type of injury is common and usually heals well over several weeks with the right care.

An ultrasound has been ordered. You will have a Doppler ultrasound of the leg. This checks the muscle injury and also makes sure there is no blood clot (deep vein thrombosis) causing the swelling. Please keep this appointment.

How to care for your leg at home

Rest: Avoid running, jumping, and pickleball until cleared. You may walk as comfort allows.
Ice: Apply an ice pack (wrapped in a thin towel) to the sore area for 15–20 minutes several times a day for the first few days.
Compression: Wear the elastic wrap or compression stocking as directed to help control swelling. It should be snug but not painful or numbing.
Elevation: When resting, raise your leg above the level of your heart to reduce swelling.
Movement: Gentle ankle movement is fine. Once the sharp pain settles, begin gentle calf stretching and gradually increase activity.
Medication for pain

Take ibuprofen 400 mg by mouth for pain as directed, with food.
Do not take ibuprofen if you have kidney problems, stomach ulcers, or are told to avoid it. Do not exceed the dose on the label without medical advice.
Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is an alternative if you cannot take ibuprofen.
Important: A water pill (diuretic such as furosemide) is not recommended for this type of swelling, because the swelling comes from the muscle injury itself, not from extra body fluid.

Return to the ER or call your doctor right away if you have:

Increasing pain that is severe or not controlled by medication
The calf becoming very tight, hard, tense, or numb, or tingling in the foot
New or worsening swelling, redness, or warmth of the calf
Pain or swelling spreading, or new chest pain or shortness of breath (possible blood clot)
Fever
Coldness, paleness, or inability to move the foot or toes
Follow-up: Keep your ultrasound appointment and follow up with your doctor or an orthopedic/sports medicine provider for recovery and a return-to-activity plan.
